item.title: CPPA Proposes Amendments to Opt-Out Preference Signal Regulations
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Tonsager and Marissa Uri
item.description: The California Privacy Protection Agency (“CPPA” or “Agency”) staff has released a package of proposed amendments to the California Consumer Privacy Act (“CCPA”) regulations governing opt-out preference signals (“OOPS”). The proposal would expressly identify the Global Privacy Control (“GPC”) as an example of a signal that businesses selling or sharing personal information must process as... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
The California Privacy Protection Agency (“CPPA” or “Agency”) staff has released a package of proposed amendments to the California Consumer Privacy Act (“CCPA”) regulations governing opt-out preference signals (“OOPS”). The proposal would expressly identify the Global Privacy Control (“GPC”) as an example of a signal that businesses selling or sharing personal information must process as a valid opt-out request, add new illustrative examples addressing when a business must process the OOPS signal as a valid sale/share opt-out, and expand the CCPA’s metrics-reporting obligations. The revised text, together with a staff recommendation that the CPPA Board advance the package to formal rulemaking and open a 45-day public comment period, is expected to be taken up at the Board’s November 5–6 meeting.

As we previously reported, the CPPA finalized updates to its existing CCPA regulations last year. The OOPS proposals build on that framework and, notably, tie several new obligations to already-adopted audit and assessment requirements. We summarize the background and key amendments below.

Background

At its November 7, 2025 meeting, the Board directed staff to conduct preliminary rulemaking activities on OOPS. According to the rulemaking materials, staff conducted stakeholder outreach, reviewed 376 pages of public comments, examined enforcement experience, and performed a state-by-state analysis of “universal opt-out mechanism” laws in other states. Staff presented its findings at the Board’s August 6–7, 2026 meeting, after which the Board instructed staff to prepare the materials necessary to open formal rulemaking.

The Agency frames the problem in enforcement terms: the Initial Statement of Reasons states that, since 2020, enforcement actions by the Agency and the California Attorney General “have demonstrated that many businesses fail to detect, honor, or properly implement” OOPS. The Agency also indicates that the additional guidance is meant to reduce businesses’ confusion about compliance obligations. The proposal arrives as the Agency-sponsored Opt Me Out Act, which requires browser developers to offer GPC functionality, is set to take effect on January 1, 2027.

Key Amendments

Express recognition of GPC. The proposal lists GPC as an example of a commonly recognized signal.

Browser features must forward the signal. Browser features that interact with businesses on a consumer’s behalf and make personal information available “must not prevent, interfere with, contradict, or disable” the consumer’s OOPS from being sent.

Metrics reporting. Annual metrics reporting—currently limited to businesses handling the personal information of 10,000,000 or more consumers—would extend to any business required to complete a cybersecurity audit or risk assessment, and covered businesses would separately report opt-out requests received through an OOPS.

Clarifying revisions. Technical clean-up changes would be made to sections 7060, 7122, 7124, 7157, 7221, and 7222. These changes include adding a “to the best of my knowledge” qualifier as part of the cybersecurity audit attestation. The Agency concluded that the economic impact of the proposal will not be significant. According to the Initial Statement of Reasons, the only amendments expected to result in measurable cost are the expanded metrics-reporting requirements.

New Illustrative Examples

New examples signal how the Agency expects businesses to operationalize existing obligations:

  • Cookie syncing. A business that receives an OOPS must prevent third-party trackers on its site from initiating or performing cookie syncing for cross-context behavioral advertising.
  • Pseudonymous, cross-device profiles. A business that links a consumer’s devices into a pseudonymous profile (e.g., via fingerprinting) must apply a GPC signal from one device to all linked devices.
  • Unlinked data. A business that keeps data in unlinked, device-specific form need apply the signal only to that device and need not collect additional information to link devices.
  • Timing of signal detection. Because GPC arrives with the browser’s initial request, a business must check for the signal before any cookies or pixels that sell or share personal information activate.

Next Steps

Agency staff recommends that the Board advance the draft regulations to formal rulemaking and initiate the 45-day comment period. If the Board votes to proceed, the draft Notice of Proposed Rulemaking contemplates a public hearing and written comment period (dates to be set), and any sufficiently related modifications would be made available for an additional 15-day comment period before adoption.

Staff has separately presented recommendations to the Board on reducing friction in the exercise of privacy rights (including clarifying how intentional interactions and cookie preferences relate to opt-out of sale/sharing) and on notices and disclosures. These topics may proceed on separate tracks.

item.title: Algorithmic Pricing Laws: A Growing State Patchwork and What Businesses Should Know
item.dc:creator: Laura Kim, Lindsey Tonsager, Jayne Ponder, Jehan Patterson and Irene Kim
item.description: Lawmakers and regulators at both the state and federal levels are increasingly focusing on consumer protection considerations relating to algorithmic pricing. On September 25, the Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) closed the comment period on a proposed enforcement policy statement on personalized pricing. The proposed statement is the FTC’s preliminary view on whether personalized pricing practices... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
Lawmakers and regulators at both the state and federal levels are increasingly focusing on consumer protection considerations relating to algorithmic pricing. On September 25, the Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) closed the comment period on a proposed enforcement policy statement on personalized pricing. The proposed statement is the FTC’s preliminary view on whether personalized pricing practices could be deceptive or unfair, and on when the agency would expect an affirmative disclosure when personalized pricing is used. The FTC’s proposed policy statement drew more than 4,500 comments from a variety of perspectives, such as small businesses, food, and technology. Many commenters raised concerns about the statement’s current broad scope, including whether the FTC would distinguish between use cases involving personal data to provide individualized price increases on the one hand and discounts or other savings or promotions that lower prices for consumers on the other. Commenters also urged the agency to preserve loyalty programs and other long-standing practices in which companies provide tailored pricing to certain customer segments.

On October 28, 2026, the FTC announced it is also conducting a market study of certain participants to understand whether industry utilizes personal data to set pricing and compensation. This follows the Commission’s earlier study on personalized pricing from 2024 and the FTC staff’s publication of initial findings from that study.

If it becomes final, the FTC’s policy statement would serve as a federal counterpart to New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, and Maryland, which have all enacted laws that address these practices and many more states that have proposed legislation. The legislative trend is also extending to the local level, with Seattle becoming the first city to prohibit certain algorithmic pricing practices. Generally, these laws target the use of personal data and algorithmic tools to set individualized prices. However, there is significant variation in the legal approaches:

  • Sector-specific bans (New Jersey, Maryland, Seattle). New Jersey’s Fair Price Protection Act prohibits using “surveillance pricing” to determine or vary the sale price of groceries and other foodstuffs based on personal data. Maryland’s Protection from Predatory Pricing Act prohibits food retailers and third-party delivery providers from using “dynamic pricing” to set higher prices for covered grocery items. Seattle’s ordinance prohibits a delivery service provider, mixed-use grocery business, or a grocery business that has 20 or more retail locations globally from using “algorithmic-based price discrimination.”
  • Disclosure (New York). New York’s law applies across sectors and requires businesses to clearly disclose when they are using personalized algorithmic pricing. The New York legislature also passed amendments that would shift away from a disclosure-based approach and instead prohibit “surveillance pricing.”
  • Ban and Disclosure (Connecticut). Connecticut prohibits retail sellers and third-party delivery services from using algorithmic pricing for any purpose other than setting a discounted price, subject to exceptions. Where an exception applies, the business must disclose: “This price was increased using your personal data”.

Key Challenges

Broadly-drafted laws may sweep in and even prohibit common pricing strategies that benefit consumers, such as personalized coupons, loyalty rewards, and targeted discounts. Exceptions for discounts are not uniform across jurisdictions.

Accordingly, given the patchwork of state algorithmic pricing laws and the potential for federal enforcement if the FTC policy statement is finalized, businesses should determine whether they are a covered entity, what practices may be impacted by these laws, whether there are any statutory exceptions that would apply, and identify the marketing collateral and pricing flows that may require updates to comply with bans or disclosure requirements.

item.title: A Comparison of the EU Cloud and AI Development Act Requirements Against the U.S. FOCI Regime and FedRAMP
item.dc:creator: Ashden Fein, Heather Finstuen, Ryan Burnette, Jacob Crump and Alexandra Bruer
item.description: As governments increasingly focus on cloud security and sovereignty, the European Commission (“EC”) is, through its proposal for a Cloud and AI Development Act (“CADA Proposal”), attempting to create a regime establishing “sovereignty” requirements on cloud computing service providers that can be procured by the public sector.  In our prior blog post, we discussed the... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
As governments increasingly focus on cloud security and sovereignty, the European Commission (“EC”) is, through its proposal for a Cloud and AI Development Act (“CADA Proposal”), attempting to create a regime establishing “sovereignty” requirements on cloud computing service providers that can be procured by the public sector.  In our prior blog post, we discussed the proposed regime in greater detail.  This proposed regime shares some characteristics with U.S. regimes for government contractors.  However, while similarities exist, there are also meaningful differences.  Existing and potential government contractors providing cloud services and operating in both the United States and European Union (“EU”) may be interested in understanding how existing U.S. requirements compare to the CADA Proposal — which requirements carry across regimes and which requirements are net new.

In this blog post, we provide a brief overview of (1) the CADA Proposal and certain existing U.S. frameworks, namely (2) the U.S. foreign ownership, control, or influence (“FOCI”) regime and (3) the U.S. Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (“FedRAMP”).  The overview is followed by a high-level comparison of these frameworks. The comparison below focuses on the scope of the respective frameworks and their treatment of provider location, data residency, foreign-government access, and the potential for foreign control to affect service continuity.  This discussion focuses principally on the FedRAMP Rev. 5 framework.

CADA Proposal

The CADA Proposal sits at the heart of the EC’s broader Tech Sovereignty Package and aims to address what the EC perceives as two critical vulnerabilities in the EU’s digital landscape: a structural deficit in data center capacity and a dependence on a limited number of non-EU cloud computing service providers.  If enacted, among other things, contractors would be required to meet the requirements of the CADA Proposal in order to provide cloud services to public-sector bodies operating in certain sectors (at the national, regional, local, and municipal government level).  The cloud sovereignty framework established by the CADA Proposal creates four “Union Assurance Levels” (“UALs”), where UAL 1 presents the least restrictive requirements and UAL 4 presents the most restrictive requirements.

FOCI Regime

The existing U.S. FOCI regime, which is governed by the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (“NISPOM”), 32 C.F.R. Part 117, applies principally in connection with U.S. government contracts or agreements that require a contractor to access classified information and therefore require the contractor to obtain a facility security clearance (“FCL”).  The FOCI regime applies when there is access to classified information by a contractor regardless of the nature of the product or service. The FOCI regime is intended to mitigate the risk of unauthorized access by foreign persons to classified information through companies performing on U.S. government contracts as well as prevent foreign persons from adversely affecting those companies’ performance on classified contracts.  To obtain an FCL, or to maintain an FCL following certain material changes to the business (e.g., a change in ownership), a contractor must submit information about foreign ownership and other relationships and undergo an assessment for FOCI.  If the U.S. government identifies FOCI, the U.S. government will require the contractor to implement mitigation measures, assuming mitigation is feasible, prior to granting the contractor an FCL to perform on the contract or to continue performing on existing classified contracts.   (Note that a FOCI mitigation determination is based on a risk assessment reflecting multiple factors.  There may be circumstances where mitigation is not feasible, including due to the sensitivity of the assets or risk profile of the source of FOCI.)

Of note, Section 847 of the Fiscal Year 2020 National Defense Authorization Act (“NDAA”) would extend the concept of FOCI mitigation to certain unclassified Department of War (“DoW”) contracts and subcontracts valued above $5 million.  More information on the forthcoming regulations implementing Section 847 is available in our client alert here.

FedRAMP

FedRAMP provides a standardized security assessment and authorization framework for cloud services that process or store unclassified U.S. government information on behalf of a U.S. federal agency, subject to specified exclusions.  In order to provide cloud services to most U.S. federal agencies, a contractor must comply with the FedRAMP requirements and obtain a FedRAMP authorization.

Comparison of Frameworks

Scope of Application

The three frameworks differ in terms of the government entities they apply to, the flexibility that they afford to address risks, and the nature of how the requirements apply.  Specifically, all three frameworks apply at the federal or national level, but the CADA Proposal would apply more broadly to cloud services procured by public-sector bodies across the EU, including not only national but also regional, local, and municipal government authorities that are responsible for various types of critical infrastructure (e.g., various types of transport infrastructure, healthcare, drinking / waste water operations, postal services, waste management, and research).  Additionally, the CADA Proposal would impose a wide range of obligations on cloud computing service providers in order for them to be certified to a particular UAL, whereas the FOCI regime and FedRAMP expressly govern contractor eligibility and foreign ownership, control, or influence risks, or assess the security of a particular cloud service offering, respectively.

Substantive Obligations

In addition to the differences in the scope of application, the frameworks also differ in terms of substantive obligations, notably including differences in their treatment of foreign ownership and control, as discussed further below.  Below we provide a non-exhaustive list of some of the key differences between those substantive obligations, focusing on issues related to the location of the provider, data residency, and the ability of foreign governments to access data / disrupt services.

  • Location/Ownership of Provider: The CADA Proposal generally requires the provider, relevant subcontractors, and supporting infrastructure to be located in the EU.  With respect to the FOCI regime, only a U.S. entity may hold an FCL, but foreign ownership or control of a cleared U.S. entity is generally permitted, subject to the feasibility of mitigating identified FOCI.  By contrast, FedRAMP does not currently have any standard restrictions on the location/ownership of the corporate entity providing services.  A few exemplary requirements are shown below.
  • Data Residency: The CADA Proposal imposes broad EU data residency requirements across all UALs.  FedRAMP generally does not impose comparable requirements, although forthcoming requirements for the highest certification class impose certain U.S. jurisdiction-based location requirements and federal agencies can impose more specific residency requirements.  Individual DoW contracts may impose additional U.S. data location requirements.  While the FOCI regime does not categorically impose a data residency requirement, required mitigation may effectively localize data within the United States.  A few exemplary requirements are shown below.
  • Foreign Government Access to Data:The CADA Proposal restricts qualification for UAL 2 unless a provider can demonstrate that it has implemented the necessary measures to ensure that access to data from a non-EU government is prevented.  A provider that is subject to foreign control is disqualified based on non-EU control at UALs 3 and 4, although a provider controlled outside the EU may qualify for UAL 3 if the applicable third-country laws meet specified standards, including that the third country does not impose measures that conflict with EU requirements governing lawful access to non-personal data.  The FOCI regime assesses the particular FOCI risk and may permit that risk to be addressed through entity-specific mitigation that may limit foreign government access to data maintained by the U.S. company.  FedRAMP does not restrict provider access or control.  A few exemplary requirements are shown below.
  • Foreign Government Ability to Disrupt Service: The CADA Proposal contains specific requirements addressing the risk that a non-EU government or company could disrupt cloud services.  For certification to UALs 1 and 2, the CADA Proposal requires cloud service providers to take steps to minimize the potential impact of that foreign control in certain domains.  For certification to UAL 3, specific laws in a foreign country (e.g., a requirement that the EU provider comply with restrictive measures from the non-EU country such as sanctions or export controls) prevent a company from even being considered as a potential service provider; although, a provider controlled outside the EU may qualify for UAL 3 if the applicable third-country laws meet specified standards, including that the third country’s legal framework cannot compel a provider to disrupt services or withhold state-of-the-art technologies from EU customers.  Foreign control is an absolute barrier to certification to UAL 4.  By contrast, the FOCI regime addresses identified risks through entity-specific mitigation.  FedRAMP addresses service disruption through cybersecurity controls, not specific restrictions on foreign ownership or control.  A few exemplary requirements are shown below.

item.title: New AI Transparency Requirements Enacted for Advertisers and Deployers
item.dc:creator: Jayne Ponder, Laura Kim and Irene Kim
item.description: State legislatures have passed new laws focused on disclosing the use of AI in advertisements or depictions of individuals. On September 16, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 1050, a new law requiring disclosures when certain advertisements prominently feature a “synthetic performer.”  This was one of several AI-related measures signed by Governor Newsom this year,... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
State legislatures have passed new laws focused on disclosing the use of AI in advertisements or depictions of individuals. On September 16, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 1050, a new law requiring disclosures when certain advertisements prominently feature a “synthetic performer.”  This was one of several AI-related measures signed by Governor Newsom this year, which we summarized in our prior blog post. 

  • SB 1050: California SB 1050 will prohibit a person from creating and causing to be published in an advertising medium an advertisement that “prominently” includes a “synthetic performer,” unless the advertisement contains a clear and conspicuous disclosure.  The law defines “synthetic performer” as a digital figure, voice, or representation created, in whole or in part, using generative artificial intelligence that creates the realistic impression of the audio, audiovisual, or visual performance of a human performer who is not recognizable as any identifiable natural person.  The disclosure obligation will only apply when the synthetic performer appears “prominently,” which the text clarifies means a person in the foreground and demonstrating or illustrating the product or service, or providing or voicing, or illustrating or reacting to, the on- or off-camera narration or commercial message. A violation of these requirements would qualify as a violation of California’s false advertising laws. The law will enter into effect January 1, 2027.
  • California’s law closely resembles New York’s synthetic performer disclosure statute, codified at N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law § 396-b.  The New York law similarly requires advertisers to provide a clear and conspicuous disclosure when a synthetic performer is used in an advertisement.
  • Hawaii’s Approach: Unlike California SB 1050, which focuses on AI transparency and disclosures for synthetic performers who are not recognizable as an identifiable person, Hawaii’s new statute focuses on the unauthorized use of realistic digital imitations of identifiable individuals.  Hawaii considered a similar disclosure-based framework for synthetic performers in the originally introduced version of the bill, but the state ultimately enacted a law that instead prohibits a person from knowingly publishing a realistic digital imitation of an identifiable individual without that individual’s consent when the imitation is used in connection with advertising, causes harm, or is used to facilitate fraud, defamation, harassment, or other unlawful conduct.  

Companies using generative AI in marketing and advertising should evaluate whether their advertisements trigger state-specific disclosure obligations and consider the requirements of existing consumer protection laws such as the FTC Act.  Check back here for more updates in state regulation of AI-generated advertising and content.

item.title: California Enacts New Privacy Legislation Affecting Consumer Rights, Data Brokers, and Website Tracking Litigation
item.dc:creator: Jayne Ponder, Lindsey Tonsager and Bryan Ramirez
item.description: In the final days of California’s 2026 legislative session, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a series of privacy legislation spanning consumer privacy rights, data broker activities, digital platform design, and civil remedies for website privacy litigation. Governor Newsom also vetoed a privacy measure that would have imposed broad restrictions on the sale and sharing of... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
In the final days of California’s 2026 legislative session, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a series of privacy legislation spanning consumer privacy rights, data broker activities, digital platform design, and civil remedies for website privacy litigation. Governor Newsom also vetoed a privacy measure that would have imposed broad restrictions on the sale and sharing of sensitive personal information. Notable bills include:

  • SB 923 – Expanded CCPA Deletion Rights and Online Request Methods: SB 923 expands consumer deletion rights under the California Consumer Privacy Act (“CCPA”) from information collected “from” a consumer to information collected “from or about” the consumer. Additionally, SB 923 will add that a business that operates exclusively online and has a direct relationship with the consumer from whom it collects personal information must provide an email address and make an online method, such as a webform or online portal, available for submitting requests.
  • AB 2561 – Operating System and Application Privacy Settings: AB 2561 will prohibit an operating system or application from changing that user’s affirmative “privacy setting” without the user’s consent, subject to some exceptions. The law broadly defines “privacy setting” to include any user-configurable option within an application’s privacy, or similarly labeled, menu, that governs the collection, use, sharing, disclosure, retention, or processing of personal information.
  • AB 883 – Amendments to California’s Data Broker Law: AB 883 modifies California’s data broker law and requirements for the state’s Delete Request and Opt-Out Platform (“DROP”) to shorten the period within which data brokers must process applicable deletion requests submitted through DROP from every 45 days to every 30 days. AB 883 also contains provisions designed to increase awareness and use of California’s DROP mechanism by requiring certain government officials to notify other officials of their ability to submit deletion requests through the platform. Additional background on California’s Delete Act legislation establishing the framework and a recent enforcement action can be found in prior blog posts.
  • SB 690 – Reform of California Invasion of Privacy Act Litigation: As detailed in our recent blog post, SB 690 eliminates the California Invasion of Privacy Act’s (“CIPA”) private right of action as it applies to certain pen register and trap-and-trace claims, though SB 690 does not eliminate or otherwise modify other CIPA provisions frequently asserted in online-tracking disputes.

item.title: CISA Submits Final CIRCIA Rule for OMB Review
item.dc:creator: Ashden Fein, Caleb Skeath, John Webster Leslie and Shayan Karbassi
item.description: On October 1, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (“CISA”) submitted a draft of the Final Rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022 (“CIRCIA”) to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (“OIRA”) for interagency review, marking one of the final steps before the Final Rule will be... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
On October 1, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (“CISA”) submitted a draft of the Final Rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022 (“CIRCIA”) to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (“OIRA”) for interagency review, marking one of the final steps before the Final Rule will be published in the Federal Register.  

As previously described, CIRCIA will require covered critical-infrastructure entities to report certain cybersecurity incidents within 72 hours and ransomware payments within 24 hours to CISA.  CISA published its Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“Proposed Rule”) in April 2024 and received substantial feedback from industry and trade associations regarding the proposal’s scope, reporting requirements, and overlap with existing reporting obligations.  In response to the hundreds of comments that it received, CISA held a series of town halls in June 2026 to solicit additional stakeholder input.  Covington previously summarized the town halls and steps organizations can take to prepare for the Final Rule, here.

The review by OIRA can take up to 90 days (or longer if OIRA seeks an extension), in which case the Final Rule would not be published until early next year.  While the effective date is not provided in CIRCIA, it is likely that implementing regulations will not become effective for at least 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.  The precise effective date will be included in the Final Rule text.

item.title: California Governor Signs Over 20 AI-related Bills into Law
item.dc:creator: Jayne Ponder, Diana Lee and Evan Chiacchiaro
item.description: Governor Gavin Newsom of California signed over 20 AI-related bills into law in the final days of September. Several of these bills address topics such as frontier model and generative AI oversight, AI transparency, and new requirements for use of AI in particular industries, described below. In addition to these bills, Governor Newsom also signed... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
Governor Gavin Newsom of California signed over 20 AI-related bills into law in the final days of September. Several of these bills address topics such as frontier model and generative AI oversight, AI transparency, and new requirements for use of AI in particular industries, described below. In addition to these bills, Governor Newsom also signed into law a sweeping set of AI bills relating to minors’ safety and privacy, which are described in our prior blog post, and novel frameworks related to the use of ADMT in the workplace, which we previously summarized here.

These newly passed laws include the following:

  • AI Transparency: Governor Newsom signed several laws focused on AI transparency, including amendments to the California AI Transparency Act and disclosure requirements for AI-generated advertisements.
    • California AI Transparency Act: Governor Newsom signed two bills amending the California AI Transparency Act — SB 1000 and AB 2713. Among other things, SB 1000 expands the scope of “covered providers” subject to the law by removing the requirement that the generative AI system has more than 1 million monthly visitors or users, updates requirements for the disclosure verification tools that must be made available to users, and imposes new requirements for latent disclosures. Additionally, SB 1000 imposes requirements where a covered provider knows that an identifiable third-party licensee modified a licensed generative AI system such that it no longer complies with the law. In contrast, AB 2713 amends requirements placed on “large online platforms,” including by requiring large online platforms to detect provenance data, rather than (under the prior law) requiring that the large online platform detect whether the provenance data is compliant with widely adopted specifications, among other requirements.
    • Synthetic Performers: Similar to the New York Synthetic Performer AI Disclosure Law,  SB 1050 will require a clear and conspicuous disclosure when an advertisement “prominently” includes a synthetic performer, which is defined as “a digital figure, voice, or representation created in whole or in part using generative artificial intelligence that creates the realistic impression of the audio, audiovisual, or visual performance of a human performer who is not recognizable as any identifiable natural person.” The disclosure must use wording “substantially similar” to “this performance features a synthetic performer” or “no human performer is depicted.”
  • Customer Service Chatbots: In addition to the restrictions on operators of a companion chatbot in Adam’s Law (SB 1119), AB 1609 will prohibit large private businesses from representing that a customer chatbot is a human and will require these businesses to provide a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the customer service chatbot is AI-generated and is not human, if a reasonable person likely would be misled into believing that they are interacting with a human. In addition, large private businesses will be required to make a good faith effort to connect a customer to an agent within 15 minutes after a request is made, or schedule an appointment with the customer, among other requirements.
  • Focus on Specific Industries: Several provisions will impose requirements on development and use of AI in certain industries or contexts.  For example:
    • Generative AI in the Legal Profession: SB 574 will prohibit an attorney from delegating the practice of law to generative AI, and it will impose specific requirements on the use of generative AI to assist with the practice of law, including taking reasonable steps to verify the accuracy of generative AI outputs and correcting any erroneous or hallucinated outputs, among other things.
  • Healthcare: Governor Newsom signed several measures focused on healthcare, such as AB 1979, which will prohibit healthcare providers or facilities from using or deploying AI for certain purposes including direct performance of certain clinical functions. As another example, SB 903 will permit entities that provide or facilitate psychotherapy services to use AI tools or systems only to assist in providing administrative or supplementary support, subject to additional requirements, and it will prohibit advertising or purporting to offer psychotherapy services when the services are provided through the use of companion chatbots.

item.title: California Governor Signs SB 690, Eliminating Private Website-Based CIPA Pen Register Claims and Calling for Broader CIPA Reform
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Cahoy, Lindsey Tonsager, Matthew Verdin, Jenna Zhang, Julia Barrero and Bryan Ramirez
item.description: On September 30, Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 690, a significant new law aimed at curbing the wave of lawsuits and demand letters asserting “pen register” claims under the California Invasion of Privacy Act (“CIPA”).  The legislation eliminates the private right of action for pen register and trap-and-trace claims arising from conduct occurring on internet... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
On September 30, Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 690, a significant new law aimed at curbing the wave of lawsuits and demand letters asserting “pen register” claims under the California Invasion of Privacy Act (“CIPA”).  The legislation eliminates the private right of action for pen register and trap-and-trace claims arising from conduct occurring on internet websites, online applications, or mobile applications, leaving enforcement authority exclusively with the California Attorney General.  The law goes into effect on January 1, 2027.

In signing the bill into law, Governor Newsom not only approved a substantial limitation on CIPA litigation but also issued a call to action for “additional work” on broader CIPA reform.  In an accompanying signing message, the Governor praised SB 690 as a measure addressing “the vexatious use of CIPA lawsuits and demand letters to extract settlement money” from businesses. At the same time, he emphasized that SB 690 addresses only one category of CIPA claims and urged the Legislature to revisit other CIPA provisions next year that remain “susceptible to abuse by overly aggressive litigants,” while calling for a “fair balance between protecting private information and preventing rapacious litigation.”   

As our previous coverage on SB 690 notes, the law makes the following key changes to existing state law:

  • Eliminates private lawsuits for website-based pen register claims. Claims arising from conduct “occurring on an internet website, online application, or mobile application” could be brought “only by the Attorney General.”
  • Applies to certain pending claims. The bill would apply retroactively to “any pending claim” in an action commenced on or after January 1, 2025, potentially affecting many pending lawsuits.
  • Preserves Attorney General enforcement. The bill would keep enforcement authority with the Attorney General.
  • Leaves other CIPA claims intact. The bill would not alter private rights of action under CIPA’s wiretapping provision (Section 631) or confidential recording provision (Section 632).

Looking Ahead

SB 690 represents one of the most significant legislative responses to the recent wave of website-based CIPA litigation.  While the law is likely to reshape the landscape for website-based pen register claims, Governor Newsom’s signing message suggests that broader CIPA reform efforts may follow next year.

item.title: New California AI Employment Laws: Key Requirements for Employers
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Tonsager, Jayne Ponder, Carolyn Rashby and Bryan Ramirez
item.description: On September 30, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed three laws that will regulate the use of AI in the employment context, starting in the new year. Below, we briefly summarize these developments, which we discuss in greater detail in our prior blog post. These laws join an existing body of California AI employment regulations. SB... Continue Reading…
item.content:encoded:
On September 30, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed three laws that will regulate the use of AI in the employment context, starting in the new year. Below, we briefly summarize these developments, which we discuss in greater detail in our prior blog post. These laws join an existing body of California AI employment regulations.

SB 947 (The “No Robo Bosses Act”)

SB 947 restricts employers’ use of automated decision systems (ADS), including by prohibiting certain inferences about protected status and adverse actions based on predictions that a worker will exercise legal rights. It also requires human corroboration for ADS-based disciplinary or termination decisions, mandates post-use notice when an employer primarily relies on ADS for such a decision, and includes protections against retaliation. Violations carry a civil penalty of $500 and may be enforced through a civil action or by the Labor Commissioner. SB 947 becomes operative on July 1, 2027.

SB 951 (Amendments to Cal/WARN)

SB 951 amends the California Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act (“Cal/WARN”) to require additional notice when a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is caused in whole or substantial part by AI or other automated technology. The notice must identify the displacement as technology-related and describe the affected positions, automated job functions, and technology involved. The Employment Development Department must publish summaries of these notices. Violations carry a civil penalty of up to $500 for each day of violation, and the employer will be liable for back pay and the value of benefits for the notice period (which will be reduced by other wages, voluntary and unconditional payments, and benefits provided to an employee during the period of violation). SB 951 becomes operative on January 1, 2027.

AB 1883 (Workplace Surveillance Tools)

AB 1883 restricts how employers may use workplace surveillance tools, including systems that collect employee data, activities, communications, biometrics, or behaviors. It prohibits using these tools to infer or predict emotional states or collect neural data, subject to limited safety and federal-law exceptions. Violations carry a civil penalty of up to $500 and may be enforced through a civil action or by the Labor Commissioner. AB 1883 becomes operative on January 1, 2027.

item.content:encoded:
On September 9, 2026, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (“FBI”) announced the publication of the FBI Cyber Strategy (the “Strategy”).  The Strategy, which “provides a roadmap for defending the American people and the nation’s critical infrastructure in cyberspace,” is broken into four pillars:

  1. Investigate, Disrupt, and Impose Cost on Cyber Adversaries;
  2. Support Victims;
  3. Increase Impact Through Partnerships; and
  4. Enhance FBI’s Cyber Capabilities.

The Strategy may be of interest to organizations as they develop and assess their own threat monitoring and incident response programs, particularly because of the Strategy’s emphasis on the FBI’s continued cooperation and information sharing with the private sector.  For purposes of this blog post, we have focused on the first three pillars, as the fourth pillar primarily focuses on the FBI’s internal capabilities.

Investigate, Disrupt, and Impose Cost on Cyber Adversaries

Although this pillar outlines three separate objectives focused primarily on efforts by the FBI to investigate and take action against threat actors, it also underscores the important role the private sector can play in supporting FBI operations to counter cyber threats.  The Strategy emphasizes that “[v]ictim reporting and the technical evidence that comes with it are essential” to the FBI’s efforts to investigate cyber intrusions and “fuel both individual investigations and the development of disruption operations that extend well beyond any single case.”  The Strategy notes that the FBI’s attribution of threat actors often leverages, among other things, “private-sector telemetry” and “victim reporting.”

Support Victims

This pillar expressly prioritizes supporting and working collaboratively with victims of cybercrime, including by pursuing the following four objectives:

  1. Share Cyber Threat Intelligence with Urgency: The Strategy notes that the FBI “will pursue capabilities that enable urgent, automated sharing of cyber threat intelligence with critical infrastructure owners and trusted private-sector partners.”  Specifically, the FBI will develop “automated indicator-sharing mechanisms that narrow the gap from FBI threat detection to partner notification from days to hours, and from hours to minutes” with the goal of “build[ing] the closer public-private partnership the threat demands, giving victims and trusted partners information they can use to defend systems, contain intrusions, and recover operations.”
  2. Quickly Engage After Incidents: The Strategy emphasizes that the FBI will engage victims with “urgency and operational rigor” and that the FBI “pursues the threat actor, not the victim.”  The Strategy states that the FBI “will notify victims and targeted entities directly and provide intelligence and support to help them defend, contain, and recover” when the FBI identifies that a device, network, or account is being targeted by threat actors.  The Strategy also emphasizes that the FBI will “continue to identify and proactively notify organizations that have been compromised or are at imminent risk,” and continue to invest in establishing relationships before an incident occurs.
  3. Deliver Specialized Capabilities to Victims: The Strategy notes that the FBI will continue to build specialized teams and programs to support victims.  The Strategy identifies various FBI capabilities, including the Industrial Control Systems (“ICS”) Coordinator program, which is designed to build operational technology expertise and support operators of critical infrastructure; the Recovery Asset Team, which works directly with financial institutions to freeze fraudulent transfers; and the Cyber Action Team, which leverages specialized personnel “to respond to major cyber threats and attacks against critical services.”
  4. Facilitate Reporting of Cyber Incidents: The Strategy notes that “[e]arly reporting gives the FBI the evidence, indicators, and financial details needed to advance investigations, notify other victims, and move against the actors responsible.”  To facilitate incident reporting, “all FBI field offices will prioritize building direct relationships with local businesses and organizations to ensure open channels for swift reporting of cyber incidents.”

Increase Impact Through Partnerships

This pillar emphasizes that the FBI is committed to expanding and deepening its relationships with partners, including but not limited to partners across the private sector.  This is further emphasized by the third objective in this pillar, “join[ing] forces with the private sector,” which notes that “[a] steady, two-way exchange of information between the FBI and the private sector is essential to disrupting adversary activity earlier, notifying victims faster, and disrupting infrastructure before campaigns can scale.”  Under this objective, the Strategy re-emphasizes its commitment to “forge direct relationships with industry partners,” including establishing “open channels of communication” and “trusted points of contact before a crisis hits.”

The Strategy further emphasizes that the FBI will seek to strengthen its existing engagement with the private sector through established programs and the expansion of its executive engagement channels.  Specifically, the Strategy cites three established programs (InfraGard, the National Cyber-Forensics and Training Alliance, and the National Defense Cyber Alliance) and three executive engagement channels (CISO Academy, Cyber Executive Summits, and the Leadership in Cyber program).

Conclusion

The FBI Cyber Strategy demonstrates the U.S. government’s continued focus on public-private collaboration to counter cyber and cyber-enabled threats, which was a key theme of the current Administration’s National Cyber Strategy and the National Security Presidential Memorandum on Expanding Capabilities to Combat Transnational Cyber-Enabled Crime.  Private organizations should expect continued government engagement on countering cyber threats, and should consider both the potential benefits and risks associated with such engagement.
